bece2.WhatFurtherStudyOptionsWillIHave: Applicants who have successfully completed the Diploma of Early Childhood Education and Care (CHC50121) are eligible to apply for direct entry into second year of the Bachelor of Early Childhood Education at Box Hill Institute.
bece2.Accreditation: This course is accredited by the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) and the qualification is aligned with the Australian Qualification Framework (AQF) level 7 and Box Hill Institute Graduate Attributes.

LD1101.UnitDescription:
The aim of this unit is to develop an understanding of the fundamental aspects of child development and learning from birth to age eight. It will examine development and learning from a biological, social and contextual viewpoint. The unit explores the foundations for promoting safe and healthy learning environments and the teacher’s role in planning for and scaffolding children’s holistic development and learning. It provides a basic introduction to observations and assessments for planning to achieve improved learning outcomes for children, which will be further explored in later units.
Students will develop their understanding of the interdependent nature of education and care for young children in early childhood education contexts. The importance of providing nurturing environments for the child’s brain development and the teacher’s role in developing and supporting these environments will be examined.
This unit establishes a framework to view young children’s learning and development. It sets a basis for thinking about planning for learning by drawing on a range of theories and developmentally appropriate practice, which will be further developed in later units.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Case Study 30%; Project 50%; Tutorial exercises 20%

PC1102.UnitName: Current Contexts In Early Childhood Education
PC1102.UnitDescription:
The aim of this unit is to develop an understanding of and engagement with the educational philosophies that have shaped and are shaping policies and practices in the delivery of early childhood education and care services in Australia. The unit explores the foundations of education from a societal, historical, and policy context including the conception of early education and care. A range of diverse approaches that have arisen out of different philosophical approaches to early learning are explored. Contexts surrounding children, families and communities and early childhood education and care are discussed.
This unit establishes a framework to view current pedagogical practice. It sets a basis for thinking about early childhood curriculum development and teaching to be further developed in the unit Teaching and Learning Theories Through Play (TCS2201).

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Test 30%; Project 50%; Tutorial exercises 20%

RCS1103.UnitName: Effective Partnerships In Early Childhood Education
RCS1103.UnitDescription:
In this unit the role of partnerships across early childhood services and the broader community and educational sector are examined. The role of partnerships with families is promoted as an essential factor in providing cohesive services for children and families. The role of early childhood educators is examined to determine their role in developing and maintaining relationships within and across services. The dynamics of partnerships, networks, and communities of practice and how educators may be positioned is explored. The dynamics of how power operates within and across services is highlighted. Students are to reflect on their own commitment and engagement with networks both within and across services.
This understanding is extended through participation in guided observation visits to early childhood services. This will support the student’s understanding of the wider sector and provides first-hand experience of the diversity of the sector and the multifaceted role of the early childhood teacher.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Report 30%; Report 50%; Tutorial exercises 20%

RCS1104.UnitDescription:
The aim of this unit is to develop the student’s ability to understand and develop respectful, secure and responsive relationships with children individually and with groups of children. The unit explores the relevant theories including attachment and assists in the development of the student’s understanding of how to achieve a healthy and mutually respectful relationship. Students explore the role of the teacher in developing responsive and respectful relationships with children and the impact of the learning environment on children’s behaviour.
Through the unit, students will be introduced to identifying possible underlying motivations of children’s behaviour and identifying behaviours that may be a concern. Students will begin to develop a toolbox of strategies that contributes to the foundation skills of providing direct and indirect guidance.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Report 50% Paper 50%

TCS1105.UnitDescription:
The aim of this unit is to develop the participant’s skills and knowledge in gathering, analysing and interpreting information about children’s learning. This information is then applied to design, implement and evaluate learning experiences to foster children’s learning, sense of agency and holistic development, applying a positive and inclusive approach.
The unit will foster the development of understanding of a range of approaches to documenting and monitoring children’s learning and then how to use that evidence to inform future planning for children. The unit will explore the importance of acting as a team with families and caregivers to support all aspects of children’s learning and will foster the development of skills in promoting opportunities for collaborative curriculum design.
Through planning exercises in real or simulated environments, students will practice the art of analysing their documentation to identify children’s interests, strengths and needs to set goals and design learning experiences in accordance with the early years learning frameworks and the service’s philosophy. The importance of learning through play, child-centred and teacher-initiated experiences, intentional teaching, modelling and scaffolding for children’s holistic learning and development will be explored.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Paper 40%; Case study 40%; Tutorial exercises 20%

TCS1106.UnitDescription:
This unit examines the legislative, regulatory and national quality frameworks relevant to early childhood education. It will assist in the development of the skills and knowledge necessary to ensure compliance and the development of quality practices in the early childhood services sector. Work health and safety policies, procedures and practices will be explored in the context of the small work team within an early childhood service. Individual job roles and responsibilities will be considered to identify the legal and ethical responsibilities, including exploring the concept of duty of care to children, families, colleagues, and the profession.
Researching, developing and implementing policy initiatives will be addressed along with the importance of leadership skills in motivating others to comply and modelling professionalism in the early childhood industry and workplace.
Students will explore the learning frameworks, the principles and practices, and will learn how to apply them to provide children with optimum developmental opportunities to facilitate lifelong learning.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Quiz 30%; Presentation 50%; Tutorial exercises 20%

TCDS1107.UnitDescription:
In this unit students will focus on the theories, practical integration and importance of the Performing arts (including drama, music and dance) in early childhood. Performing arts is an important language of early childhood that allows children to express ideas, feelings, relationships and experiences in their lives. Students will develop their understanding of the role of the arts in children’s expressive development and explore the links between performing arts and social and cognitive development, and as a medium for emotional and creative expression.
The importance and use of performing art from a cultural viewpoint will be examined. Students will explore their own artistic expression and appreciation of the performing arts to enhance their understanding of theoretical frameworks that support creative expression and employ these understandings, attitudes and skills to their planning, implementation and assessment. Students will review Gardner’s theory of multiple intelligences focussing on the intelligences relevant to the performing arts.
Students will explore and evaluate appropriate resources and a range of strategies to help empower children with materials and meaningful opportunities to guide them to individual and independent creative expression. Ways to inform and involve families in their child’s experiences with performing arts will be discussed.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Paper 40%; Presentation & plan 40%; Tutorial 20%

TCS1108.UnitDescription:
This is the first of two units exploring and understanding the role of reflective practice in teaching, learning and professional development. The unit introduces a theoretical and conceptual understanding of reflective practice and processes for engaging in reflective practice. Students will engage in thinking about the effects of their values, beliefs and behaviour on their practice.
Students will identify and explore strategies and approaches to develop themselves as reflective practitioners and begin to implement reflection to build their own teaching capabilities and ethical practices. The role of supervisors and mentors as a component of reflective practice will be explored.
This will be further developed in the second reflective practice unit during third year.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Paper 40%; Paper 50%; Tutorial exercises 20%

TCS2201.UnitName: Teaching And Learning Theories Through Play
TCS2201.UnitDescription:
This unit aims to build on the students’ understanding of how children learn. It fosters development in their understanding of how to create nurturing learning environments and the role of the early childhood teacher in achieving this. Examined throughout the unit are theories of learning through play and the implications for teaching in contemporary early childhood settings. Play-based learning will be examined as a key component of developing effective early childhood pedagogy.
Time will be spent in observation, applying and reflecting on how play-based practices and principles are demonstrated across all practicum experience settings. This will permit an examination of the learning taking place and implications for curriculum development and intentional teaching across a range of play experiences. Child-centred and teacher-led programming will be explored as participants start to develop their philosophies on learning and teaching.
The practicum placements will reinforce the focus on play as the primary pedagogy of early childhood education. Students will be supported to engage in the planning and implementation of intentional teaching during play experiences through mentoring and supervision during practicum placements. It is expected they will demonstrate their ability to engage in and scaffold children’s learning through play and start to consider documentation processes.
The practices and principles of the frameworks will be used as a guide for early childhood teaching.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: LD1101, PC1102
Assessment: Case Study 50%; Presentation 50%

LD2202.UnitDescription:
In this unit students will apply their knowledge of infant and toddler development to lead pedagogically sound infant/toddler programs. The importance of providing nurturing environments for the infant’s brain development and the teacher’s role in developing and supporting these environments will be stressed. Students will apply their understanding of developing and sustaining nurturing education and care programs that skilfully integrate care and education for infants and toddlers.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Lit review 50%; Exposition 50%

RCS2203.UnitName: Families And The Early Childhood Community
RCS2203.UnitDescription:
This unit centres on the importance of working in partnership with families in caring for and educating children. There will be a focus on strategies to establish and maintain relationships with families within the early childhood community and across the broader community. Throughout the unit there will be an exploration of the principles and values of implementing a family-centred practice approach in the delivery of services. Students will explore the social, structural and cultural diversity of families, attitudes, legislation and policies that impact on Australian families including the historical and cultural perspectives of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations and the implications for curriculum development and service delivery.
This unit will require some observation and immersion in the local community as a strategy to more fully understand the socio-cultural context of families in the area and the implications for delivering a program that supports child and family strengths.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Case study 30%; Essay 50%; Tutorial exercises 20%

PCC2204.UnitDescription:
The practicum is designed to enable the students to apply the theoretical knowledge acquired in the lectures and tutorials of the preceding units of study. As the students develop knowledge at more complex levels during the course, the practicum placement reflects this development and requires the student to engage in increasingly more complex tasks and environments. This is achieved by the sequence of and the specific requirements of each practicum experience.
During this twenty-day first practicum pre-service teachers are required to demonstrate their understanding of infant/toddler development through their teaching and learning practice, and program development appropriate to this age group. This requires pre-service teachers to demonstrate how education and care combine to create appropriate nurturing learning environments for infants and toddlers.
Pre-service teachers are to demonstrate their pedagogical practice in the infant and toddler program and to extend their understanding, knowledge, and skills required for effective early childhood teaching. Pre-service teachers will reflect on their teaching practice for this younger age group, their ability to lead infant toddler teams, and identify areas for further development.

Practicum hours: 20 days (140 hours)


Prerequisites: All first-year units must be completed prior to undertaking this practicum unit. LD2202 Leading Infant toddler programs.
Assessment: Report 50%; Reflective Journal 50%
PCC2204.Prerequisites: All first-year units must be completed prior to undertaking this practicum unit. LD2202 Leading Infant toddler programs.

TCDS2205.UnitDescription:
This aim of this unit is to develop the student’s understanding of theories of language development as well as their abilities to foster language and literacy acquisition in young children. The relationship between literacy theories and practice will be explored. The importance of oral language as a basis for literacy along with an understanding of the stages of the reading and writing processes will be examined to assist them to identify appropriate pedagogies including evaluation and assessment to meet the needs and interests of diverse young literacy learners. Students will be supported to use their developing theoretical understanding of language and literacy development to implement a range of language and literacy experiences that target children’s interests and language and literacy profiles, either in their own workplace, in a simulated environment or during practicum placements. As the students develop their philosophy of language and literacy curriculum development, the workplace provides a challenging environment to test the validity of their philosophies. They will be encouraged to implement rich literacy experiences and develop their skills in storytelling, mime, puppetry and creative writing.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: LD1101, TCS2201
Assessment: Annotated Bibliography 50%; Design an early literacy program 50%
TCDS2205.Assessment: Annotated Bibliography 50%; Design an early literacy program 50%

TCDS2206.UnitDescription:
The aim of this unit is to extend the student’s theoretical knowledge and practical skills related to teaching and learning mathematics with young children. Students will analyse how young children develop their mathematical understandings and how the role of gender, culture and learning dispositions may influence the acquisition of mathematical concepts. The unit will focus on how teachers can use children’s interests and everyday experiences to explore mathematical concepts and develop problem-solving skills. There will be a focus on play-based and intentional teaching strategies.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: LD1101 TCS2201
Assessment: Portfolio 50%; Paper 50%

TCDS2207.UnitDescription:
This aim of this unit is to develop the student’s understanding of theories of language development. It aims to focus on the importance of the visual arts in early childhood. Visual art is an important language of early childhood that allows children to express ideas, feelings, relationships and experiences in their lives. Students will explore the links between visual arts and social and cognitive development, with an emphasis on the importance of visual arts in the development of literacy and mathematics. Students will be introduced to an understanding of the importance of the visual arts as a medium for emotional and creative expression.
The importance and use of visual art from a cultural viewpoint will be examined. Students will explore their own art practices and response to aesthetics to enhance their understanding of theoretical frameworks that support creative expression and art making and employ these understandings, attitudes and skills to their planning, implementation and assessment with young children. Students will be introduced to the stages of young children’s drawing and make links with literacy development. They will be introduced to a range of strategies that are appropriate to help support children with materials and guide them to develop independent expressions and problem solving skills. Ways to inform and involve families in their child’s experiences with visual arts will be discussed.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: LD1101 TCS2201
Assessment: Portfolio 50%; Paper 50%

PCC2208.UnitName: Professional Practice Placement 2 (Three Year Old Preschool)
PCC2208.UnitDescription:
The practicum is designed to enable the students to apply the theoretical knowledge acquired in the lectures and tutorials of the preceding units of study. As the students develop knowledge at more complex levels during the course, the practicum placement reflects this development and requires the student to engage in increasingly more complex tasks and environments. This is achieved by the sequence of and the specific requirements of each practicum experience.
This practicum is a twenty day placement to be completed with three year old children attending a funded three year old preschool. The aim of this is to build on the students’ knowledge and experience and requires that they apply their increasing understanding of early childhood pedagogy to curriculum development, documentation, implementation and evaluation across a range of specific tasks. Early childhood pedagogical practices related to these tasks have been delivered through the pre-requisite units for this placement. Support for developing sound pedagogical practice will continue to be provided through the BHI academic supervisor and host placement supervisor (Fieldwork mentor), including creating positive learning environments, finding the balance in providing experiences that challenge, yet are achievable and support the children’s holistic development. In this practicum students are also expected to demonstrate their increasing ability to design experiences, based on assessment and focussed on learning goals and children’s interests. Students share with staff the rationale and implementation strategies required to achieve the identified outcomes. The students reflect on their teaching practice and identify areas for improvement.

Practicum hours: 20 days (140hr)


Prerequisites: PCC2204 Professional practice placement 1 (Birth – three years) and all other second-year units must be completed prior to undertaking this unit.
Assessment: Observation and planning 50%; Reflective Journal 50%
PCC2208.Prerequisites: PCC2204 Professional practice placement 1 (Birth – three years) and all other second-year units must be completed prior to undertaking this unit.

LD3301.UnitDescription:
This unit provides the theoretical foundations to enable students to plan holistically for children enrolled in three-year old and four-year old preschool programs. It follows on from the learning and development as well as the teaching and curriculum studies units in the previous two years. The unit examines the milestones of physical, social, emotional, psychological, language and cognitive development of this age group. Strategies to create engaging learning environments that maximise learning outcomes will be identified. Students will analyse contemporary early childhood frameworks and curricula to assist them to plan innovative, inclusive preschool curriculum.
The theoretical learning in The Preschooler unit will provide the foundational knowledge necessary to successfully complete the requirements of the PCC3307 Professional practice placement 3.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Case Study 50%; Paper 50%

TCS3302.UnitDescription:
This unit aims to extend the student’s understanding of challenges facing children growing up in contemporary Australia. It will strengthen their ability to take a critical stance on local and global issues and how these issues may be incorporated in the early childhood program. The role of advocacy for children and children’s rights will be addressed, along with development of the teacher’s identity as an agent of change.
Students will be challenged to extend their understanding of the importance of the structure and management of learning environments. They will examine the role of the adult in developing and maintaining positive learning environments in early childhood settings, and their role in resourcing parents to support their children to develop social competence and cooperative and responsible behaviours. Students will be asked to identify possible causes of dysregulated behaviours and strategies to apply to assist the child to achieve or re-establish self-regulation. The unit examines effective guidance strategies to develop an environment that supports children’s learning and well-being. This unit, and the related practicums, aim to enable them to practice and bring together their understanding of the importance and power of creating positive learning environments for children’s well-being and learning.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Paper 50%; Presentation 50%

TCS3303.UnitDescription:
This unit investigates a range of approaches for assessing, recording and reporting on children’s learning to inform teaching practice and meet organisational requirements. The unit examines assessment design and implementation principles that relate to early childhood contexts and inform early childhood teaching practice. This unit builds on learning in prior units, which have introduced students to the concepts of documentation and assessment. This unit expects a higher level of investigation and implementation to achieve the expected learning outcomes.
This unit provides important instruction and skill development necessary for completion of the tasks in the preschool professional placement, and also for teaching practice upon graduation. The documentation requirements of a registered early childhood teacher are significant, and the transformational learning achieved through this unit will provide the student with excellent foundations for their future practice.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Case study 50%; Paper 40%; Forum 10%

TCS3304.UnitDescription:
This is the second of two reflective practice units. It aims to extend the student’s knowledge and understanding of reflective practice to support the development of more critical thinking when engaging in reflection. This unit aims to progress the student from a technical interpretation of reflection to an examination of self as impacting on learning and relationships.
The unit aims to support the students to develop and articulate a personal philosophy for teaching and learning by reflecting on contemporary theories, pedagogies and their own practice. The students will also investigate the role of reflective practice in demonstrating teacher professional standards and quality practice as outlined in the National Quality Framework (NQF).

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: TCS1108
Assessment: Paper 50%; Paper 50%

TCDS3305.UnitDescription:
This unit aims to extend the student’s theoretical knowledge and practical skills related to the use of Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs) in teaching and learning with young children. Students will analyse how young children develop skills in the use of ICTs and how ICTs can be used to complement teaching and learning in early childhood environments. Students will be supported to advance the children’s understanding of ICTs by introducing a new application of ICTs within the integrated program either in their own workplace, a simulated environment or during practicum placement.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Debate 30%; Presentation 30%; Paper 40%

TCDS3306.UnitName: Science And Environmental Studies In Early Childhood
TCDS3306.UnitDescription:
The aim of this unit is to extend the student’s theoretical knowledge and practical skills related to science and environmental studies teaching and learning with young children. Students will analyse how young children develop their science understandings and develop a sense of wonder and empathy for the world around them. Students will be required to demonstrate increasing skill in questioning technique to support the children’s learning and developing sense of enquiry. Students will also be required to demonstrate increasing skills in planning to facilitate the children’s sustained engagement with exploration of concepts in a range of science experiences integrated across the curriculum.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Presentation 50%; Paper 40%; Forum 10%

PCC3307.UnitName: Professional Practice Placement 3 (Four – Five Year Old Preschool)
PCC3307.UnitDescription:
The practicum is designed to enable the students to apply the theoretical knowledge acquired in the lectures and tutorials of the preceding units of study. As the students develop knowledge at more complex levels during the course, the practicum placement reflects this development and requires the student to engage in increasingly more complex tasks and environments. This is achieved by the sequence of and the specific requirements of each practicum experience.
In this twenty five day practicum unit, pre-service teachers undertake the Four-five year old preschool practicum. Pre-service teachers are required to demonstrate their ability to assume the role of an early childhood teacher in a sessional preschool environment. This includes the ability to create a positive learning environment and encourage strong learning dispositions for children.
In this practicum, pre-service teachers are to bring together all the knowledge gained in units studied to develop and maintain safe and challenging learning environments for children. Under the guidance and supervision of the host placement supervisor (Fieldwork mentor), pre-service teachers are to assume responsibility for the planning, delivery and evaluation of the preschool program. This includes assessment, documentation, program planning, and teaching across all aspects of the program, and communication with families, and staff. Pre-service teachers are responsible for the professional climate and running of the program, ensuring compliance with regulations, and adherence to national quality standards and service policies. Pre-service teachers will be expected to reflect on the role of manager, team leader or preschool director to gain a clearer understanding of the management role assumed by teachers, particularly in stand-alone kindergarten or preschool programs. Support for understanding legal and ethical responsibilities, including compliance and management will be delivered in pre-requisite units. Models of assessment, program development documentation, and teaching theories will be explored in practice throughout the placement.
Pre-service teachers are supported with individual supervision sessions specifically aimed to assist them to apply the theoretical aspects of their course work to the practicum requirements.

Placement: 25 days (175 hours)


Prerequisites: PCC2208 LD3301 TCS3302 TCS3303
Assessment: Plan, implement, and evaluate educational program 40%; Reflective Journal 60%
PCC3307.Assessment: Plan, implement, and evaluate educational program 40%; Reflective Journal 60%

RCS3308.UnitDescription:
This unit sits within the learning and development stream and will examine the biological, psychological, and developmental factors that affect children’s learning. This unit will build on the student’s theoretical knowledge of child development and its articulation into practical skills when responding to diverse groups of children. Social, cultural, and environmental factors will be looked at in relation to program provision for children across the full range of abilities and additional needs. This will include, but is not limited to giftedness, culturally and linguistically diverse learners, developmental delay, sensory impairments, or chronic ill health.
Students will examine their own values in relation to difference and their role in promoting inclusive practice in their centres and the wider community. Students will analyse methods in developing inclusive learning practices, including the modifying of the learning environment, utilising the service system and working with a wide range of specialists to achieve maximum outcomes for children and their families.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: LD3301 TCS3302 TCS3303
Assessment: Paper 50%; Presentation 50%

TCS4401.UnitDescription:
The unit aims to develop the student’s ability to work with children and families with Indigenous backgrounds. It will explore the issues faced by First Nations people, both current and historical which directly influence their participation in early childhood services and the wider community. It will consider the particular learning needs of children and the family’s needs for respectful partnerships and communication.
The unit explores authentic ways to integrate Indigenous culture and approaches into the early childhood curriculum. Students will look at ways to create culturally inclusive classroom environments. Anti-bias approaches to curriculum development, delivery and assessment will be discussed. Strategies and resources available to educators will be explored and evaluated.
The students will examine the importance of working closely with not only children, but also families/caregivers and the wider community. The importance of maintaining and developing the home language and culture of children will be explored.

 


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Report 50%; Paper 50%

PC4402.UnitDescription:
In this unit students will examine and analyse theories and issues of leadership in the dynamics of the early childhood organisational context. The unit requires students to engage with, and reflect on, the meaning of leadership in the context of early childhood professional practice, ethics, identity and relationships. The five faces of leadership will be used as a construct for students to analyse their own leadership capacities across the multiple roles that early childhood professionals adopt. The unit explores contemporary issues regarding leadership and change and the implications for management. The role of advocacy as a critical face of leadership and the role of leadership in providing effective and ethical governance will be examined.
Students will explore organisational behaviour theories and concepts in complex work environments. They will examine individual and group behaviours in organisational settings and be introduced to tools to critically examine their oral and written communication and interpersonal skills.
This unit will explore various aspects of organisational workplaces to assist students to develop the necessary skills to work in and lead effective teams.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Case Study 40%; Position Description 30%; Paper 30%

LD4403.UnitName: The Child In The Early Years Of School
LD4403.UnitDescription:
This unit provides the theoretical foundations to enable the students to interact effectively with and understand the essential factors in creating positive educational environments for children in the five to eight year old age group. It specifically addresses the needs of children and families making the transition to school and assists the student to develop effective transition plans. Students will use the Early Years Learning Framework, and the Essential Learning Standards (foundation level) as guiding documents to prepare the child for transition. Individual differences and cultural influences will be emphasised. They will apply this knowledge to assist them to further develop a developmental child profile.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: LD3301
Assessment: Paper 30%; Presentation 50%; Case study 20%

PC4404.UnitDescription:
This unit extends the theoretical informants related to a range of organisational demands and higher-level approaches to management in early childhood education and care settings. Particular emphasis will be on human resource and management issues specific to children’s services. The unit aims to enhance managerial competence through applied management principles and practices that create sound effective management of children’s services organisations. Students will examine management theories and their application to organisational policies and procedures, supported by the legal and industrial frameworks relevant to early childhood education and care services. Additionally, students explore Occupational Health and Safety responsibilities, evaluation of policies against industry standards, quality assurance, and remaining current and connected to the wider early childhood and educational community. The professional responsibility for interpreting and implementing legislative and other relevant guidelines and policies are examined. Students reflect on their preparedness to adopt a management role and, in the final stages of the degree, how their management skills can be further developed.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Project 50%; Reflection 40%; Forum 10%

PCC4405.UnitDescription:
The practicum is designed to enable the students to apply the theoretical knowledge acquired in the lectures and tutorials of the preceding units of study. As the students develop knowledge to more complex levels during the course, the practicum placements reflects this development and requires the student to engage in increasingly more complex tasks and environments. This is achieved by the sequence of and the specific requirements of each practicum experience. This practicum has two components to it: transition practicum of 5 days and a preferential practicum of 10 days.
Transition Placement:
In this professional experience placement the aim is for students to gain an increasing understanding of the multiple roles of preschool teachers. It is designed to provide students with the opportunity to gain rich insights into the impacts of the transition period for young preschool children and their families. Further, through analysis of the collaboration processes in place between the preschool and primary school teachers they reflect on the transition period from multiple perspectives. This placement also provides the opportunity to identify considerations for preparing a child for a smooth transition to the next phase of formal education and critically examine the role of transition plans in action. This will also be used to nurture their own skills in writing transition plans and reports. It is envisaged that students will undertake this practicum in a range of ways that reflect the children’s individual situations and the arrangements in place in both the preschool and receiving school. It is expected that the student will actively participate as is appropriate in the transition program. The student has been allocated 5 days to undertake this component of the practicum.
Preferential Placement:
This placement is of the student’s own choice in collaboration with BHI to ensure that proper supervision can be provided. Appropriate placements include early intervention services, specialist placements such as an educational unit at a hospital, zoo or museum, council, or other early childhood education programs for specific populations. The aim of this practicum is to provide students with the opportunity to extend their specific interests in early childhood teaching, management or administration in a supported teaching environment. The student has been allocated 10 days to undertake this component of the practicum.

Placement: 15 days (105 hours)


Prerequisites: TCS4401 PC4402 LD4403 PC4404
Assessment: Interview 10% Report 20%; Report 10% Proposal 10%; Reflective journal 50%
PCC4405.Assessment: Interview 10% Report 20%; Report 10% Proposal 10%; Reflective journal 50%

PC4406.UnitDescription:
In this unit students examine research approaches that can support their professional learning and improve their professional practice. Students will be introduced to steps in designing an action research project, methods of data collection, how to organise and interpret information, and reporting findings to relevant stakeholders. The student will also be required to investigate key ethical considerations in early childhood research.
The action research project will critically examine an aspect of the development, implementation, and/or evaluation of a centre/service program or process that significantly contributes to, extends, or improves professional practice. By negotiation, students may use this unit to take up a placement in a specialised setting; an alternative Early Childhood Education and Care program, or an interstate or international location. The project will be undertaken under the supervision of a Box Hill Institute staff member and, if involving placement in a specialised service, a representative from that workplace. The student will be required to present a project proposal and plan, and submit the outcomes of the project in an appropriate report.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Proposal 30%; Project 30%; Report 40%

PC4407.UnitDescription:
This unit is a threshold unit. It aims to assist the student to transition from the pre-service teacher to the graduate early childhood teacher. It fosters the student’s knowledge of professional practice skills and ongoing professional learning. It aims to assist the student to think beyond the teaching role to look more broadly at their place as a professional in the early childhood sector. It introduces the student to industry organisations, their function and available professional resources and their importance in supporting and enhancing the profession. It offers an opportunity to refine their application and interview skills and assists them to establish skills required to continuously develop their professional practice. Students will enhance their skills in forming plans for professional development. They will be introduced to the purpose and importance of performance appraisals and the need for effective inter-personal communication skills in this process. The unit will discuss the importance of a healthy work-life balance and managing stress.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: PCC3307
Assessment: Portfolio 50%; Case study 20%; Essay 30%

LDTC4408.UnitName: Recognising, Understanding And Responding To Trauma
LDTC4408.UnitDescription:
This unit provides the theoretical foundations to enable the students to closely examine the biological, psychological, cognitive and developmental factors that affect the learning and development of children who have experienced or are experiencing trauma. This unit prepares early childhood teachers to identify and respond to a variety of trauma types, including those specific to child abuse, Indigenous issues and refugee issues. The aim of this unit is for the students to build a more complex understanding of child development and learning and the articulation of their knowledge into practical skills when responding to children in the early childhood setting who have or are experiencing trauma. This includes theories of attachment, and the socio-cultural aspects that influence children’s development. It builds students’ knowledge and skills in recognising trauma, and their ability to understand the contexts in which it may occur throughout the topics covered. Students will analyse a range of strategies in a variety of early childhood settings for supporting children who have experienced trauma. Students will also examine the effects of their own behaviour on children experiencing trauma and how the child’s effective recovery can be influenced by educator responses. Students will examine their own values in relation to trauma-related issues in the lives of young children and their role in promoting healing and recovery within the early childhood setting. Students will analyse practices involved in creating safe, nurturing environments to promote recovery, including modifying curriculum, utilising the service system and working with a range of specialists to achieve maximum positive outcomes for children and their families.
Students will also learn a range of strategies for self-care in relation to their own emotional responses to children experiencing trauma.

Contact hours: Face-to-face: 6 hours of lectures, 12 hours tutorials, 6 hours workshop.  Online: 12 hours tutorials.


Prerequisites: nil
Assessment: Forum 10%; Presentation 40%; Case study 50%

bhm02.WhatDoesThisCourseInvolve:
Take our hospitality management degree and increase your chance of securing a position to manage large operations in the hospitality industry. 
Our course has a strong focus on practical learning and, with our small class sizes, you can tailor your individual learning based on your needs and with one-on-one support from lecturers. 
In our hospitality management course, you’ll develop skills in: 
- accounting 
- marketing 
- business and hospitality law 
- workplace communications 
- strategic project management 
- contemporary issues in hospitality 
- contemporary human resources management 
You'll also have the opportunity to practise your skills with a work-based hospitality management project. 
If you have completed an accredited diploma or advanced diploma in tourism/events or hospitality, you may receive credit towards this degree.

Graduates will have: 
- a broad and coherent body of knowledge, with a deep understanding of the underlying principles and concepts in one or more disciplines as a basis for independent lifelong learning

- cognitive and creative skills to exercise critical thinking and judgement in identifying and solving problems with intellectual independence 
- communication skills to present a clear, coherent and independent exposition of knowledge and ideas

- learn effective study skills to help you in the classroom 
- build confidence to join higher education, training, or professional courses 
After an assessment, you will be placed in the course that best matches your skills: 
- English for Academic Purposes 1 
- English For Academic Purposes 2 
These courses give you the support you need to take the next step in your study or career.

BUS101.UnitDescription:
This unit introduces the underlying conceptual framework, general concepts, principles and practices of accounting, and incorporates such knowledge in decision-making by stakeholders. The unit also incorporates the fundamental elements of accounting and provides a practical understanding of how business transactions are treated and recorded in the financial statements. Students will also learn how to evaluate organisational performance through the analysis of financial statement information.

The aim of the unit is to develop an understanding of how accounting information and financial statements can inform decision making by internal and external stakeholders of organisations. The unit is also designed to build knowledge upon which useful financial information is sourced, prepared, and presented, with the application of basic accounting principles and standards.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Invigilated Test 20% | Assessment 2: Accounting Decision Making Business Report (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Examination 40%
BUS101.Assessment: Assessment 1: Invigilated Test 20% | Assessment 2: Accounting Decision Making Business Report (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Examination 40%

BUS102.UnitDescription:
This unit teaches foundational concepts in marketing and their application in the modern world. Topics covered in this unit are marketing concepts, environments, principles, practices, techniques, marketing campaigns and strategies and develop the marketing mix to provide customer value. Students will also learn about digital communication, presentation skills and discipline knowledge that are imperative to the marketing profession.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Weekly activities, test or quizzes (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Case Study (Individual) 40% | Assessment 3: Marketing Project (Group) 40%
BUS102.Assessment: Assessment 1: Weekly activities, test or quizzes (Individual) 20% |	Assessment 2: Case Study (Individual) 40% | Assessment 3: Marketing Project (Group) 40%

BUS103.UnitDescription:
This unit provides the foundational knowledge and skills of management, which includes an understanding of management theory, the fundamental concepts of management, the four functions of management, globalisation and the issues relating to the management of organisations both locally and globally (multinationals & emerging markets). The unit covers different management approaches, organisational needs, internal and external challenges & risks, governance, and ethics needed to run an organisation. Management skills will be developed with a reflective emphasis to enable students to identify future roles as managers or managers of organisations.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Weekly activities and quizzes (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Case Study (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Management Project (Individual) 40%
BUS103.Assessment: Assessment 1: Weekly activities and quizzes (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Case Study (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Management Project (Individual) 40%

BUS104.UnitDescription:
This unit offers an introduction to Information and Communication Technology (ICT) systems.  Students investigate the nature, types, concepts, issues and benefits of ICT and their impact on business processes and organisations. Students will learn the importance of ICT to decision-making through analysing data & information by identifying, reporting, and managing risk. The unit offers an understanding of ICT abilities and their limitations and how it enhances the efficiency and effectiveness on an organization.The relevance for current ICT system trends, likely future developments and ICT for improvement will be examined.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Weekly activities and 4 quizzes (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Business Information Systems Project (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Individual. Examination 40%
BUS104.Assessment: Assessment 1: Weekly activities and 4 quizzes (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Business Information Systems Project (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Individual.  Examination 40%

BUS105.UnitDescription:
This unit provides an introduction to the key elements of effective communication in a business environment and online communication by exploring communication theory, frameworks and principles. Principles of effective workplace communication including verbal, non-verbal, oral, written, formal and informal as well as active listening skills are covered. Also, collaboration, co-operation, teamwork, cultural and language differences will be covered by this unit. Students will develop skills in effectively addressing workplace communication gaps including researching, organisation, negotiation, conflict management, resolution, persuasion and interviewing techniques.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Individual Portfolio (Individual) 40% | Assessment 2: Workplace Communication (Group) 20% | Assessment 3: Workplace Communication Project Report (Group) 40%
BUS105.Assessment: Assessment 1: Individual Portfolio (Individual) 40% | Assessment 2: Workplace Communication (Group) 20% | Assessment 3: Workplace Communication Project Report (Group) 40%

BUS106.UnitDescription:
This unit offers an introduction to the Australian legal system, as well as some basic legal principles and areas of law which are closely related to the commercial transactions and business activities. Topics include: the legal systems, contracts, consumer protections, the law of negligence, business entities, the law relating to the incorporation of companies, agency and partnership, and the law of sale of goods.

Students will learn legal knowledge and develop their practical skills in the application of key legal principles in business activities such as professional accounting operations.  The unit will provide skills in researching laws, checking contracts, forming businesses, and navigating legislative requirements to support business transactions.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Invigilated Test (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Assignment (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Examination (Individual) Open book 40%
BUS106.Assessment: Assessment 1: Invigilated Test (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Assignment (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Examination (Individual) Open book 40%

BUS107.UnitDescription:
The unit provides a theoretical and practical understanding of the importance to exercise appropriate ethical judgements in the complex and globalised business environment. The unit introduces numerous ethical/moral frameworks in analysing various ethical issues, corporate governance and concerns faced by management. This unit aims to develop a practical approach to business decision making by adopting and applying appropriate ethical decision-making framework to ethical dilemmas. Analytical and critical thinking skills will be developed to assist in the identification, analysis and resolution of ethical issues. Students will be able to incorporate the skills developed through this unit into their workplace, understand the importance of ethics and apply it in a professional capacity.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: In-class test (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Case Study (Individual) 40% | Assessment 3: Business Ethics Project (Group) 40%
BUS107.Assessment: Assessment 1: In-class test (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Case Study (Individual) 40% | Assessment 3: Business Ethics Project (Group) 40%

BUS108.UnitDescription:
This unit provides an introduction to a broad range of microeconomic and macroeconomic concepts, theories and analytical techniques. Demand, supply, and market equilibrium analysis will be used to model the fundamental trade-offs and choices that are ubiquitous in daily lives via the comparison of costs and benefits of actions. Microeconomics discusses the production and market structure at the firm level. Aggregate demand and supply models will be used to illustrate several macroeconomic issues. The unit examines macroeconomic objectives and the role of government policy to address market failures. Students will develop an understanding of the nature of economic decisions and the relationship between the macro and micro perspectives of economic activity.

Students will develop interpretation skills of economic conditions in local and international contexts and access knowledge to relevant economic data and information. They will develop review skills they can apply when reviewing the nature and impact that government policy interventions have on the economy.  Students will use economic concepts to improve decision making in business and government.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: In-class test (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Case Study Analysis Project (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Examination (Individual) 40%
BUS108.Assessment: Assessment 1: In-class test (Individual) 20% | Assessment 2: Case Study Analysis Project (Group) 40% | Assessment 3: Examination (Individual) 40%

BUS201.UnitDescription:
Design Thinking is the innovative approach to developing business solutions to complex problems (strategic, operational or organisational) and bring new products or services to market. Design thinking reframes problems and prioritises ideas into optimal innovative solutions through human-centred processes.

This unit endeavours to provide a working knowledge of the key elements, methodologies, supporting tools and techniques of Design Thinking. Key concepts explored include ideation and prototyping, creative thinking, ill-structured problem solving, collaborative/participatory, and human centeredness. The importance of embedding Design Thinking as an organisational process which establishes innovation as a core part of a business is also investigated. Students will have the opportunity to develop their design thinking competence through application to projects in order to consolidate understanding.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Wicked Problem Article Analysis 30% | Assessment 2: Group Literature Review 30% | Assessment 3: Group Design Challenge Project 40%
BUS201.Assessment: Assessment 1: Wicked Problem Article Analysis 30% | Assessment 2: Group Literature Review 30% | Assessment 3: Group Design Challenge Project 40%

BUS202.UnitDescription:
This unit introduces data analysis concepts, tools, roles and responsibilities used by a Data Analyst. The fundamentals of data analysis, data gathering, databases, data warehouses & data mining will be covered as well the difference between the roles of a Data Analyst, Business Analyst, Data Scientist, and Data Engineer. 

Students will learn to identify data sources, clean, analyse and effectively communicate the meaning of data to stakeholders through the use of visualizations and dashboard tools. 

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Test (1.5 hour) (individual) 30% | Assessment 2: Data Communication Project (individual) 30% | Assessment 3: Group Case Study Analysis 40%
BUS202.Assessment: Assessment 1: Test (1.5 hour) (individual) 30% | Assessment 2: Data Communication Project (individual) 30% | Assessment 3: Group Case Study Analysis 40%

BUS203.UnitDescription:
This unit is designed to provide detailed knowledge and understanding, as a foundation, for initiating, planning and managing projects (implementing, controlling and closing). The unit also equips students with the skills needed to manage challenges with projects in variety of contexts. Emphasis is placed on teaching project management (PM) processes such as selecting the right projects which bring the maximum value, as well as the completion of a project and the realisation of the project objectives.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x1hr practical/tutorial

This unit will develop the key skills needed for working with and across cultures. Students will explore cultural theories, concepts and frameworks to understand perspectives on culture, values and identity. In focusing on individual case studies from countries around the Asia-Pacific (including Australia) students will develop an appreciation of how historical, social, economic and political forces shape culture and identity, and will leave the unit with enhanced cultural knowledge, cross-cultural communication strategies and a deep understanding of the international environment in the Asia-Pacific.

The foundational models needed to successfully unlock the innovative and creative capacity in commercial pursuits will be explored. Students will develop specific knowledge and understanding of the global and Australian hospitality industry; current trends and forces that are shaping the hospitality and tourism industry; the industry’s growth during the twenty first century into a position of economic significance; and the challenges this growth presents for the future. HOSH202.UnitName: Financial Management For The Hospitality Industry
HOSH202.UnitDescription:
Students are introduced to a range of financial tools and techniques to enable them to make informed decisions based on financial information that relate to businesses within the hospitality and tourism industry.

Key accounting concepts, principles and analytical tools and financial models are explored and applied incorporating industry standard assumptions to build skills in financial decision making for both short term and long term business planning.

A critical topic is the management of working capital and the importance of the liquidity for the hotel organisation to remain solvent. Furthermore, sophisticated pricing models are introduced together with costing tools that aid managers make informed decisions on how to increase room revenues for the hotel property.

The time value of money (TVM), internal rate of return (IRR) and Price Index (PI) financial models are explored extensively for long-term strategic capital investment decisions.

Assessments are developed to instil critical thinking and complex problem solving that a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) or a department manager will face on a daily basis in managing the finances of a large and complex organisation such a hotel or a resort.

bit01.WhatDoesThisCourseInvolve:
Technology is transforming every industry, creating exciting career opportunities for graduates with the right mix of technical expertise, practical experience, and industry insight. Our Bachelor of IT is designed to prepare you for a successful career in one of Australia's fastest growing sectors. 
With a strong focus on Cyber Security, cloud technologies, networking, systems administration, and emerging digital solutions, you'll graduate with the skills employers are looking for and the confidence to contribute from day one. 
Industry Connected Learning 
At Box Hill Institute, you'll learn through real world projects, industry standard technologies, and hands on practical experience. We work closely with leading technology partners including Microsoft, AWS and Cisco to ensure our curriculum reflects current and emerging industry needs. 
You'll gain experience using professional tools, platforms, and equipment while learning from lecturers with industry expertise. Throughout the course, you'll have opportunities to engage with industry, develop practical solutions to real problems, and build a portfolio of work that demonstrates your capabilities to future employers. 
Practical, Hands On Experience 
This degree combines theory with extensive practical learning, helping you build job-ready skills in areas such as: 
- Cyber Security 
- Network Security 
- Cloud Computing 
- Virtualisation Technologies 
- Systems Administration 
- Network Administration 
- Internet of Things (IoT) 
- Emerging Digital Technologies 
You'll learn in specialist laboratories, work with industry standard software and hardware, and develop the technical and professional skills needed to thrive in today's technology workforce. 
Australian Computer Society (ACS) Accredited 
This course is accredited by the ACS, Australia's leading professional body for the technology sector. 
ACS accreditation provides confidence that the course meets nationally recognised standards for ICT education and industry practice. For students, this offers several important benefits including: 
- recognition of your qualification by employers across Australia and internationally 
- confidence that the curriculum aligns with industry expectations 
- enhanced graduate employability through alignment with professional standards 
- a pathway to ACS professional membership and ongoing professional development 
- support for graduates seeking careers in global technology organisations 
Choosing an ACS accredited degree means studying a program that has been independently reviewed for quality, relevance, and industry alignment.

A Degree Designed for the Future.  Technology continues to evolve, creating exciting opportunities for graduates who can combine technical expertise with critical thinking and problem-solving skills. 
Whether your goal is to protect organisations from cyber threats, manage cloud infrastructure, develop digital solutions, or support emerging technologies, the Bachelor of Information Technology provides the knowledge, practical experience, and industry connections to help you launch a successful career.

BIT101.UnitDescription:
This unit gives an overview of the principal areas of Cyber Security. It covers the seven domains of systems security as identified by the International Information System Security Certification Consortium (ISC)². The areas covered include cyber security analysis, controls and operations, various cyber security threats, various threat mitigation techniques, and responding to cyber-attacks.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Group Assignment on Current Cybersecurity Issues 30% | Assessment 2: Practical Skills Exam 30% | Assessment 3: Final Examination 40%

BIT102.UnitDescription:
This unit covers fundamental cloud computing topics as they pertain to both technology and business considerations. It covers Software as a Service (SaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS) and Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) Cloud Delivery Models and public, private, hybrid and community clouds. External issues, such as service level agreements, privacy, security and legal requirements are addressed. The unit includes vendor-independent courseware from EMC. It also includes a practical component based on vendor-specific cloud frameworks, such as Google and/or Amazon clouds.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Lab Exercises 20% | Assessment 2: Group Research Assignment / Presentation (1500 words per person) 30% | Assessment 3: Final Examination 50%
BIT102.Assessment: Assessment 1: Lab Exercises 20% | Assessment 2: Group Research Assignment / Presentation (1500 words per person) 30% | Assessment 3: Final Examination 50%

BIT103.UnitDescription:
In this unit two aspects of business management will be examined: organisational leadership and financial planning. Styles of organisational structure, strong leadership and the effective management of people will also be explored. Some theoretical concepts will be introduced related to the various categories of management style and positional hierarchies of people in organisations, however, strong emphasis will be placed on observing and reporting on ‘real examples’ in order to demonstrate the value of these concepts. Students will investigate the principles of sound business accounting practice and financial planning, and introduce various tools of financial planning and analysis.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Tutorial presentation (1000 words and 5 minute presentation) 30% | Assessment 2: Tutorial presentation (1000 words and 5 minute presentation) 30% | Assessment 3: Major project 40%

BIT104.UnitDescription:
This unit provides a solid basis for students in networking and routing. This will involve an examination of networking from the OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) seven-layer model and TCP/IP perspectives. Students will learn the function and operation of appropriate equipment from each layer. Presented with a small to medium network specification, students will perform the task of commissioning a network themselves.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Case Study and Investigative Report (Group Assignment) 30% | Assessment 2: Practical Examination 30% | Assessment 3: Final Examination 40%

BIT105.UnitDescription:
This unit provides an introduction to computer systems hardware and architecture, and the fundamentals of operating systems. Using the PC as an example of a modern computer system, the unit will include the various aspects of hardware construction, fault-finding and commissioning. Suitable hardware devices and associated software will be selected, installed and commissioned to meet a given set of specifications. This is followed by the installation and configuration of a typical operating system, with emphasis on the abstraction layers it provides to the associated hardware.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr practical/tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Weekly Tutorial / Quiz 30% | Assessment 2: Practical Assignment on Operating System Configuration and Scripting 30% | Assessment 3: Final Examination 40%
BIT105.Assessment: Assessment 1: Weekly Tutorial / Quiz  30% | Assessment 2: Practical Assignment on Operating System Configuration and Scripting 30% | Assessment 3: Final Examination 40%

BIT106.UnitDescription:
This unit is intended to introduce the student to the contexts and activities of Systems Analysis and Design. The objective of this unit is to equip students with fundamental investigation and planning activities associated with the development and maintenance of information systems. Informed decision-making, new or changed business processes and data collections by representing the essence of the business activities as a number of simple diagrammatic models are covered. Abstract diagrammatic models enable evaluation of the impacts of the proposed new system or agile augmentations to current system prior to making decisions about the development or extension of information systems.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: In-class tests 30% |Assessment 2: Abstract Modelling Report 30% | Assessment 3: Final Examination 40%

BIT107.UnitDescription:
This unit provides students with an introduction to computer programming. It is assumed that students will have little or no previous programming knowledge. The basic concepts of programming will be covered including data types, selection, iteration, input/output, file handling, arrays and the basics of object oriented programming. This unit provides the foundation for the other more advanced and specialised programming units.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr practical


Prerequisites: None

BIT108.UnitDescription:
This unit introduces students to the concept of the database, its use as a repository of organisational information, and to basic technical requirements of database management. Relational models of data will be used to design databases from stated business requirements, how to create and populate database tables, modify table contents and interrogate tables in order to report the organisational information held within the database. The administration of users and security will also be covered, and Structured Query Language (SQL) used to create, populate and interrogate relational databases, and non-relational databases also investigated.

 

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr practical/tutorial

BIT201.UnitDescription:
This unit looks at the ethical implications of the widespread use of ICT systems and how governance frameworks are used to guide businesses in the ethical use of ICT. ICT professional knowledge, including professional practice responsibilities, and ICT professional ethical and legal issues will be covered in detail. Student’s will further develop their interpersonal and organisational communication skills, knowledge and understanding of IT governance and ICT service management that graduates will require in professional practice.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr tutorial


Prerequisites: None
Assessment: Assessment 1: Weekly Labs / Quiz 20% | Assessment 2: Ethical Analysis Report 30% | Assessment 3: Case Study Report 50%

BIT202.UnitDescription:
This unit is designed to provide the knowledge and how to apply in practice as required by professionals in any discipline as a foundation for working on, initiating and managing organisational projects. Project management methodologies such as PMBOK, Prince2 and Agile will be explored, and the staged nature of projects and the processes within the project stages analysed. The characteristic techniques that have application in the processes of project management will be explored, such as Cost Benefit Analysis, Critical Path Method (CPM), Gantt Charts, Risk Analysis, Resource Scheduling and Load Balancing.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr tutorial


Prerequisites: BIT103 Business Management

BIT301.UnitDescription:
This unit introduces students to entrepreneurship, innovation and new ICT venture management in today’s business world. The unit will cover how to leverage business management knowledge and use it successfully in entrepreneurial ventures with a key focus on the development of enterprising and entrepreneurial attitudes, skills and behaviours to ensure the effective establishment of management and work, regardless of the organisational context.

BIT302.UnitDescription:
This unit provides an opportunity for students to put into practice the theoretical and practical knowledge acquired during the course and their major study. Working in groups, each group will undertake a project relevant to their major to create a new ICT product or improve an existing ICT product. Each project will go through the various system development life cycle stages including executed project planning, design, implementation, and testing. Students will present their project outcomes and demonstrate the working product during a seminar arranged by a project coordinator at the end of the semester.

BIT203.UnitDescription:
This unit looks at the various network security issues, including malicious activities targeted to identify existing vulnerabilities of a computer network. Following on with theoretical knowledge of various technical methodologies and management policies designed to protect a computer network from such activity, the emphasis of this unit will be on the application of theoretical knowledge to configure a secure network within a laboratory environment. Advanced techniques in network security and its practical implementation will also be covered.

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr practical


Prerequisites: BIT104 Networking and Routing Basics

BIT204.UnitDescription:
Common Cyber Security attacks involve weaknesses and exploits in operating systems and services such as web servers and databases. This unit looks at typical problems with configuration and deployment of these systems and considers how to harden them against attack. Detection and response systems, such as intrusion detection are also covered, with consideration of security controls and their use in managing risk.

 

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr practical


Prerequisites: BIT105 Computer Architecture and Operating Systems
Assessment: Assessment 1: Penetration Testing Report (1500 words) 30% | Assessment 2: System hardening Report (2000 words) 40% | Assessment 3: Final Examination 30%

BIT205.UnitDescription:
Cyber security governance specifies the accountability framework and provides oversight to ensure that risks are adequately mitigated, while management ensures that controls are implemented to mitigate risks. Management recommends security strategies. Governance ensures that security strategies are aligned with business objectives and consistent with regulations. This unit examines both governance and its realisation in management, covering legal requirements, business constraints and policies, and cyber security resources.

Subject contact hours (per week):

2x2hr lecture; 2x2hr tutorial


Prerequisites: BIT101 Overview of Cyber Security

BIT206.UnitDescription:
The aim of this unit is to enable students to plan, implement, optimise, secure and maintain a network server operating system infrastructure. Topics include, how to plan, design, implement, analyse and configure core server functions, as well as design and implement a directory service solution.
Students will consolidate knowledge and skills of these concepts with hands-on laboratory work.

BIT207.UnitDescription:
This unit introduces students to the fundamental concepts of data analytics through real-world case studies and examples. Students will learn about data analytics project lifecycles, the difference between data analytics, data science, and machine learning; building an analytics framework, and using analytic tools to draw business insights.

BIT208.UnitDescription:
Statistical methods are key components for data analysis and this unit introduces formal statistical methods for data analytics. Students will be introduced to exploratory data analysis approaches, a key preliminary step for understanding the data, and the concept of random sampling, an important requirement to reduce bias and yield a higher quality dataset, even with big data. The unit will also include the principles of experiment design for providing definitive answers to questions, and use of regression analysis approaches to estimate outcomes and detect anomalies. Key classification techniques for predicting which categories a record belongs will also be covered.

Subject contact hours (per week):

1x2hr lecture; 1x2hr practical/tutorial

BIT209.UnitDescription:
This unit introduces the tools and techniques of data analytics with the application to business intelligence. Students will be introduced to the descriptive and predictive tools for data analytics, as well as the technologies, applications and practices needed for the collection, integration, analysis, and presentation of business information. How to facilitate effective implementation of organisational strategies through better business decision making will also be covered.

BIT210.UnitDescription:
This unit introduces students to the foundations, state-of-the-art models and techniques and applications of machine learning and artificial intelligence technologies. Capabilities, strengths and limitations of various artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques will be explored, and students will have the opportunity to apply appropriate artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning algorithms to solve complex real world problems.
